title: Modeling Requests, Latency, and Throughput

sections.title: Shortening the Time on the Scarce Resource
Capacity Planning for a New Service

html:
With the flag switched off, the product-page team met to plan the second rollout, and the whiteboard filled with proposals. One engineer wanted more Recommendation Service replicas. Another wanted a bigger connection pool. A third pointed out that both would open more sessions on a database whose limits the team had never measured. Every proposal rested on a guess about traffic, about how long each lookup occupied its connection, and about what the database could take, and none of those guesses was written down.

This chapter turns those guesses into a small model you can work through at a whiteboard. It works for a feature you are adding to a running service, and it works just as well for a service that does not exist yet.

Request Rates Across Dependencies

Let’s consider the request path from Chapter 1. Every product page needed a catalog lookup, while only pages selected by the feature flag requested recommendations. A cache hit might avoid a database read, and a retry could add another database call without adding another customer. The rate that matters depends on which resource we are sizing. For the connection pool, it is the rate at which handlers acquire connections.

A page request may trigger several outbound calls, and some calls may use the database more than once. That is why the API request rate alone cannot size the pool. We need the acquisition rate measured at the pool itself.

Concurrency and Resource Occupancy

A database connection is unavailable to another request while a handler uses it, so demand on the pool depends on two things, how often handlers take a connection and how long each one has it. Double either number and, on average, twice as many connections are busy.

The relationship is known as Little’s Law:1 L=λW.L = \lambda W.L=λW. Here LLL is average concurrency, λ\lambdaλ is the completion rate, and WWW is the average time an operation spends inside the measured boundary. For a database connection pool, that interval starts when a connection is assigned and ends when it is returned.

Applied to the Chapter 1 instance, about 400 lookups a second, each occupying a connection for about 70 milliseconds, the law gives an average of 28 busy connections out of the 40 allowed. On paper that leaves a comfortable margin. In production, lookups arrived in bursts, and a burst only a little larger than average filled the other 12 connections and started the queue the engineers found. That is why we use the equation to estimate average demand and then test the bursts and long-running operations that an average cannot describe.

Both numbers must come from the same boundary. If you multiply the request rate for the whole fleet by the occupancy measured on one instance, you get the connections the entire fleet needs, and comparing that with one instance’s pool of 40 makes the instance seem twenty times overloaded. The diagram in Figure Figure shows how request, worker, and database boundaries differ.

Shortening the Time on the Scarce Resource

One practical option is to release a connection earlier. Let’s consider a handler that prepares its request payload while the connection is already assigned.

with pool.acquire() as conn:
    payload = build_payload(request)
    result = query_database(conn, payload)
payload = build_payload(request)
with pool.acquire() as conn:
    result = query_database(conn, payload)

The second version prepares the payload before acquiring the connection, freeing the connection for other requests during that preparation. We would first verify that payload construction does not depend on data that must be read or locked within the transaction. The improvement comes from shortening connection occupancy, and the production metric can confirm whether it was meaningful.

Fleet Capacity and Failure Conditions

Little’s Law gives an average, but the hours that test a system are rarely average. A promotion, a nightly batch run, or a fleet recovering from an outage can push demand well above it for minutes at a time. When an instance fails, the others receive more requests, and the load balancer may distribute them unevenly. We therefore need to test the proposed configuration during a realistic peak, during a deployment, and with fewer healthy instances. A limit that survives all three conditions is one the team can safely operate with.

The database is shared by every application instance, so per-instance limits must fit within a fleet-wide allocation. A deployment can briefly run more pods than the desired replica total because Kubernetes permits surge capacity.2 Increasing the connection pool without checking that combined limit may make the database less responsive. PgBouncer, a connection pooler that sits in front of PostgreSQL, can let many application connections share fewer database sessions. That relieves the session limit, but every query still runs on the same database CPU and disk, so it leaves query throughput where it was.

Decision review

Which capacity limit applies to the fleet?

Twenty instances may each open 40 database connections, 800 in total, while the database allocates 600 sessions to this service. A rollout can run additional instances. The team proposes more replicas to improve latency.

Increase the replica total because CPU use is low.

First set a fleet-wide connection budget and test throughput under the expected instance and deployment configurations.

The second choice addresses the shared limit. More replicas increase the total number of sessions even when individual instances have spare CPU. With a budget in place, the team can reduce per-instance pool limits, shorten connection occupancy, or introduce a connection pooler such as PgBouncer, and then test the resulting database throughput.

The same principle applies to availability zones. A test with every instance healthy cannot establish what happens when a zone becomes unavailable. The capacity test must include the smaller surviving fleet and the recovery traffic it receives.

Load-Test Saturation and Admission

The estimate gives us a starting configuration. The load test checks whether it serves the required traffic when requests overlap and some operations take longer than their average. Table Table shows an illustrative test of one instance with a 40-connection pool, run open loop, as Chapter 1 described, so that the offered rate does not fall when responses slow down.

Illustrative steady load-test stages. Each stage must also confirm that unfinished requests are not accumulating.
Offered/s Completed/s Rejected/s Acquire p95
300 300 0 2 ms
400 400 0 8 ms
480 470 10 25 ms
560 440 120 80 ms

In the final test stage, more traffic produced fewer successful completions. Connection-acquisition time and rejections also increased. That is the behavior the team needed to identify before expanding the rollout. The knee of a throughput curve is the region where additional demand stops producing a comparable increase in completions.

For this release, the team required the 95th percentile (p95) of connection-acquisition time to be below 50 ms and rejections below one percent. The 400 stage passed. At 480, ten requests a second were rejected, about two percent of the offered load and twice the allowed rate, even though acquisition time was still below its threshold. The team ran further stages between 400 and 480, repeated them with one instance removed, and set each instance’s admission limit just below the highest stage that passed both checks. That tested rate became the allocation from which the per-instance limits in Chapter 1 were derived.

The test also gives us a basis for choosing a correction. If the database has spare query capacity, a larger pool may reduce acquisition waits. If locks or long transactions limit throughput, adding sessions can make latency worse. Caching can reduce repeated reads, while a durable queue may be appropriate when the API can accept a task for later completion. We will explore those choices in Chapters 5 and 12.

Capacity Planning for a New Service

For a new design, we may have requirements rather than production metrics. Imagine a platform receiving measurements from thousands of sensors. Devices that lose connectivity may upload buffered readings when they reconnect. The useful design concern is whether an ingestion service can accept those readings durably while downstream processors catch up, and what response devices receive when admission is limited.

An ingestion API might acknowledge a reading once it is durably accepted, then process it asynchronously. For independent jobs handled by one consumer group, a managed queue such as Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) may be sufficient. Kafka becomes a candidate when multiple consumers need a retained stream, per-device ordering within a partition, or replay. Both designs require duplicate handling and a recovery plan. PostgreSQL could store device metadata, while object storage could retain raw readings for later reprocessing. Chapter 12 develops the queue and event-log alternatives.

For audit ingestion, file processing, or webhook delivery, the architecture changes with the durability promised at acceptance. If the API reports that a task was accepted, it needs a durable record and a recovery path even when the downstream consumer is temporarily offline.

Summary

The most useful idea in this chapter is also the simplest. Demand on any shared resource comes from two numbers, how often work arrives and how long each piece of work occupies the resource, and both have to be measured at the same place. Once you think that way, the whiteboard debate from the start of the chapter changes character. A bigger pool, more replicas, a shorter transaction, and a cache stop being opinions and become different ways of changing one of those two numbers, each with a cost you can name.

Two cautions go with it. An average describes a quiet day, so every estimate needs a test at peak traffic, during a deployment, and with part of the fleet missing. And per-instance settings add up, so the question is always what the whole fleet can open against the shared database, not what one instance can open.

Everything here assumed that a request either finishes or fails while the caller waits. Calls to other systems break that assumption, and payments break it most painfully, because a caller can give up without learning what happened at the other end. Chapter 3 takes Baodium’s checkout into that uncertainty.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & The planned replica fleet can meet request demand during deployment surge and an instance failure without exceeding the shared database allocation.
Condition that tests it & Traffic peaks, a replica failure, or deployment overlap increase the request rate or the number of connection pools running concurrently.
Constraint or invariant & The combined fleet connection limit must fit the database allocation while leaving capacity for other applications and recovery.
Evidence and uncertainty & The illustrative load test completed 400 requests per second without rejection and showed increasing acquisition delay at higher offered rates. Twenty pools of 40 could permit 800 sessions against a 600-session allocation even before deployment surge.

Still unknown: the sustainable completed rate and acquisition delay during uneven routing, instance failure, and deployment overlap.
Signal and evaluation window & Measure offered requests, completions, rejections, pending operations, connection acquisition, and database sessions during each tested stage.
Control and decision & Apply a fleet-wide connection budget and test the surviving replica population. If the limits fail, reduce occupancy, reduce database demand, or change the tested database allocation before increasing admission.
Owner and review trigger & The service owner validates the workload. The database owner confirms the shared allocation. The release owner evaluates deployment surge. Review when routing, replica totals, or transaction occupancy change.

  1. J. D. C. Little, “A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L=λWL=\lambda WL=λW,” Operations Research, 1961. It concerns long-run averages in a stable system.↩︎

  2. For a Kubernetes Deployment using a percentage for maxSurge, Kubernetes rounds the allowed surge up. Chapter 10 examines rolling deployment settings and their resource consequences.↩︎
